/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.headline: Ofcom reports falls in harmful content as it opens TikTok investigation
/society/2026/oct/23/uk-children-just-as.bodyHtml:
Ofcom launched an investigation into TikTok in July over child safety concerns, including how it checks whether users are adults or children, and has recorded some reductions in harmful content on platforms including the games Minecraft and Call of Duty, and on YouTube, Pinterest and Facebook. Even so, the UK’s online regulator admits that landmark online safety measures have overall failed to limit the proportion of children suffering harm from social media – an assessment branded “staggering” by campaigners.

That overall finding comes from an Ofcom review of the first nine months of supposedly strict requirements on social media platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, which found that the proportion of children being fed unsafe content that often left them frightened, confused and upset was almost unchanged.

Under the Online Safety Act, the tech giants had to protect children from harmful content including pornography, serious violence, suicide material, racism, misogyny and bullying, with a series of specific duties introduced in summer 2025.

But Ofcom found that “at a total level there was no significant change in the proportion of children encountering harmful content over the first nine months after the children’s safety duties came into force in July 2025”.

It called the finding “concerning” and said there was no evidence indicating a change in the severity of harm since the flagship regulations, under the Online Safety Act, took effect.

Examples of harms included children being shown the murder of Charlie Kirk, graphic pornography and weapon-related content making them feel unsafe in their schools and neighbourhoods. Personalised recommendation feeds powered by “for you” algorithms were repeatedly found by Ofcom to be at the root of the continuing tide of harmful material.

The findings come a week after a coroner concluded that access to the suicide-related material on TikTok may have played a significant part in the decision of Adriana Retyte, a 14-year-old pupil at Langley school in Norfolk, to take her own life in May.

They come a day after Clavicular, 20, a popular social media influencer who promotes surgery and drugs as part of extreme male beauty regimes and has appeared with Andrew Tate, pleaded not guilty to rape in a US court, raising fresh concerns about the influence of “manosphere” content creators.

Ofcom’s research included tracking the exposure of UK children aged eight to 17 to harmful content on user-to-user services, its impact and their use of safety tools and an analysis of children’s wellbeing after exposure to harmful content. The assessment has been shared with Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport.

NSPCC, a child protection charity, said the findings showed that children were being exposed to harmful content at an “alarming rate”, which it said was echoed in the flow of calls for help to Childline, its online and telephone support service. Rani Govender, the head of child safety online, said “progress is not happening nearly fast enough”.

“Tech companies have had months to act, yet too many platforms are still built to keep children hooked with their algorithms continuing to push harmful content to their young users,” she said. “We urgently need stronger action from tech companies to rein in features that drive harm to children and stop putting business interests over their safety obligations.”

Dame Melanie Dawes, the watchdog’s chief executive, this week told MPs: “We do not see a safety culture from these large social media companies.” The regulator is already facing a wave of legal actions from tech companies challenging its powers including the Instagram operator Meta, as well as TikTok and X, owned by Elon Musk’s SpaceX group. It has warned it risks being “absolutely clobbered legally by deep-pocketed individuals and firms”.

Children most commonly reported encountering pornographic content via personalised feeds, and girls, in particular, reported feeling confused or upset after seeing such content, Ofcom found. Suicide and eating disorder content was also driven mostly through personal feeds, with girls most likely to encounter both types of harmful material. The Ofcom review also found that “young men and boys consuming motivational and self-improvement content can rapidly become exposed to more extreme content which includes the promotion of misogyny and racism”. Misspelled hashtags and coded language are often used to bypass content moderation systems that would otherwise block harmful misogynistic content.

Ian Russell, the father of Molly Russell, who took her life aged 14 in 2017 after viewing suicide material on social media, told the Guardian the lack of progress was “staggering but sadly not surprising”. He blamed “timidity and lack of action” from the regulator and said: “It is time that Ofcom stood up for children and investigated the major flaws in TikTok and Instagram’s design features, not just small technicalities that have been their focus so far.”

An Ofcom spokesperson said: “This is an industry that’s been unregulated and unaccountable for more than 20 years. And so while significant progress is being made – including the introduction of widespread age checks, stronger protections against grooming, and tougher safeguards against child sexual exploitation and abuse – we’re under no illusion that there is much for the industry still to do. We’ve shown that tech firms that don’t comply with their duties can expect enforcement action.”

It said the data did not cover the period from this spring when it said it stepped up pressure on Facebook, YouTube, Snap, Roblox and TikTok over child safety issues.

The continuing risks to children come before a planned Australia-style social media ban in the UK for under-16s which is due, from next spring, to cover platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook and X, but not messaging services such as WhatsApp and Signal.

However campaigners have warned that must not overshadow the need to enforce protections under the Online Safety Act.

“Children will continue to face risks on services covered by the act but not the proposed ban, including gaming and messaging platforms,” said Mitali Sud, a senior policy manager at Internet Matters, a child online safety campaign. “Sixteen- and 17-year-olds will still use social media. A social media ban cannot replace the need to make online services safer for children.”

A government spokesperson said platforms needed to do more to protect children from harmful content.

“That’s why we are taking bold action to strengthen protections for children from risks of harm online – banning social media from offering their services to under-16s and protecting kids from harmful functionalities like livestreaming and stranger communications on a wide range of services, including gaming services,” they said.

“When it comes to children’s safety, we are not and never will be bystanders. Platforms have both a moral and legal duty to protect children and we expect them to work with us to set a new normal for future generations.”

TikTok, Meta, X and Google were contacted for comment.

/society/2026/oct/23/realistic-and-reass.headline: Shopkeepers and psychologists praise calm, proportionate response to Be Ready advice
/society/2026/oct/23/realistic-and-reass.bodyHtml:
When the UK government launched its “Protect and Survive” public information campaign in 1980 on how to stay alive after a nuclear attack, it was met with a combination of scepticism, disbelief and derision.

The advice included how to build a “fallout room” at home, how to whitewash windows to protect from a blast, and how to store a dead body for up to five days.

You might expect this would have prompted widespread panic, but in fact it led to a political backlash, and was later lampooned on TV and in music.

It shows the risks governments take when launching such campaigns, and the fine balance that must be struck between hammering home a practical message without causing panic – or other unintended reactions.

The government’s new Be Ready campaign is advising the public to stock up on three days’ worth of supplies for use during severe weather or cyber-attacks, so help can be directed to the most vulnerable first.

In a concise, two-page document, it suggests people stock bottled water and non-perishable food for three days, a torch with spare batteries, a wind-up FM radio, a first aid kit and a copy of their passport. To stave off panic buying, it advises people to check their cupboards first and build up items gradually on regular shopping trips.

While there is no evidence the advice has triggered mass panic, the public is clearly responding. Jack Brown, who co-owns Sgt Prepper Shop, which stocks emergency food and survival tools, said he received a month’s worth of orders in the first 24 hours of the Be Ready campaign.

“I thought my phone was glitching or being hacked with the number of orders coming in,” he said.

Brown said the advice seemed sensible and proportionate. Three days was the “sweet spot”, he said, with most everyday emergencies like power cuts, a burst water main or flooding sorted within that timeframe.

It is also “realistic, affordable and fits in a cupboard”, he said, adding that asking people to stock up on a month’s worth of supplies would feel overwhelming and most people would do nothing at all.

A wind-up radio was also a sensible suggestion, and ones with a built-in torch and phone-charging USB port make them “one of the most useful bits of kit you can own”, he said.

Dr Sarita Robinson, associate dean for the school of psychology and humanities at the University of Lancashire, said there was little evidence to suggest these kinds of messaging campaigns cause panic.

“There’s this perception that if we tell people the truth we’re somehow going to panic them and it isn’t the case,” she said.

“When we use accurate messaging about emergency situations, the public will engage with that proactively. It’s when we start to hide information and there’s a void of information, that’s when things can go wrong for government.”

She said Be Ready was “realistic, quite low level, and should be reassuring because it’s basically treating the public like the grownups they are”.

Dan Goss, who runs Start Prepping UK, said traffic to his website was up 700 per cent since news of the campaign emerged in August. He said he was glad to see the subject finally being taken seriously and spoken about in “plain language” by the government, and felt the risk of panic was low.

“The level of uptake required for that would be huge – you would need to have an enormous number of people all take the government’s advice very seriously and all jump on it as a priority,” he said.

“We’re definitely in a phase now where we’re seeing lots of more disruption to people’s lives – not necessarily apocalyptic disasters, but things that have a big impact on small areas, so this advice is very much needed.”

Robinson said the campaign showed how the perception of “prepping” has shifted, especially since the Covid-19 pandemic when most people will remember seeing empty supermarket shelves.

“We did a study during Covid that showed people who did mild levels of prepping, such as having food, masks and hand gel in the house a few weeks before the pandemic, had lower anxiety and depression, and less stress,” she said.

“The government really needs to portray that this is just normal, everyday, very common in other countries, and isn’t wearing a tinfoil hat and building a nuclear bunker in your back garden.”

/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.headline: National Grid restores power to tens of thousands after Storm Austen
/uk-news/2026/oct/23/storm-austen-weathe.bodyHtml:
Engineers were working on Friday to restore power after the first named storm of the year, Storm Austen, cut electricity to more than 31,000 homes in south-west England and forced schools to close.

Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning; by 3pm, more than 31,000 homes in the region were without power, according to National Grid.

Dozens of schools across Cornwall delayed their opening because of the storm, while others did not open at all; flights were also disrupted at airports in the south-west and the Channel Islands, with passengers advised to check their flight status before travelling.

Guernsey airport’s duty manager, Steve Ford, confirmed that normal service was not expected to resume before Saturday morning, with most of the fleet stranded on the UK mainland; the Dutch flag carrier, KLM, cancelled dozens of its scheduled flights for Friday and Saturday.

Images showed part of Brighton’s West Pier falling into the sea after it was battered by wind and waves. The pier, which first opened in 1866, has grown increasingly derelict since closing to the public in 1975, with storms and fires destroying much of what remained; English Heritage has previously declared the structure beyond repair.

National Rail reported severe disruption across the network, with cancellations across England, Wales and Scotland.

Forecasters have put an additional amber weather warning for wind in place from Saturday into Sunday as the second named storm of the year, Boelo, heads in.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the government was focused on readiness: “We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”

A government campaign urging people to stock supplies of food and essentials in case of multi-day emergencies made headlines overnight, as Burnham attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires; he was asked whether the government was playing catchup with civil preparedness.

He answered: “No. We are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

“We’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

“It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments [and] we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.”

National Grid said its engineers had so far restored power to more than 52,000 properties affected by Storm Austen.

In Sussex, Southern Water said it was arranging deliveries of bottled water for customers after a power cut affected a reservoir in the area.

A Met Office amber warning for wind covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly was issued on Wednesday, taking effect on Friday from 1am until 10am.

The Met Office has now issued a 24-hour amber warning for wind from Storm Boelo from 9pm on Saturday, covering Scotland, the north coast of Northern Ireland, and Cumbria and Northumberland in the north of England.

The forecaster warned of danger to life from flying debris, with gusts of up to 80mph expected to hit exposed coastal areas and winds of 60-70mph widespread elsewhere; it also said there was a “good chance” of power cuts, damage to buildings, trees being uprooted and travel disruption.

In anticipation of Storm Boelo, train lines in parts of northern and western Scotland are scheduled to close early at the weekend.

Services south and west of Kilwinning in North Ayrshire and the Oban and Mallaig lines will shut on Saturday evening, while the line between Kyle of Lochalsh and Achnashellach in the Highlands will be out of service on Sunday; trains are expected to run at reduced speed elsewhere in the country.

The Republic of Ireland’s weather agency, Met Éireann, issued six warnings of varying severity for Saturday, mostly affecting counties along the west coast.

/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.headline: Russia and Ukraine agree to local ceasefire in Oleshky to allow aid and evacuations
/world/2026/oct/23/ukraine-troops-report.bodyHtml:
The White House says Russia and Ukraine have agreed to a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, where a deepening humanitarian crisis has left thousands of civilians struggling to survive.

In a statement on Friday, the White House said both sides had agreed to halt all military operations in the city from 27 October to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and preparations for the evacuation of civilians.

Residents of the southern Ukrainian city, under Russian occupation since February 2022, have described increasingly desperate conditions amid severe shortages of food, water and electricity; an estimated 2,000 people remain in the city, with some reportedly forced to survive on weeds, boiled grass, bread and meagre rations.

Both Russian and Ukrainian officials said all sides were close to agreeing to a ceasefire.

The White House said the ceasefire was brokered by Melania Trump, whose representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms. “Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine,” the first lady said.

There had already been protracted efforts to organise a humanitarian ceasefire, despite the White House’s claim that it had been brokered by Melania Trump, with Ukrainian officials claiming it had been Russia that had rejected previous calls.

Calls for a ceasefire had also been issued by Pope Leo XIV – who discussed the issue with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy – the United Nations, EU officials and the Council of Europe. As recently as 18 October, Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, had said he thought agreement was close, without any mention of the first lady’s involvement.

Ukraine has for weeks been pushing for a civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, at times using drones to airdrop emergency food and medical supplies into the town.

Lubinets told Reuters on Friday that the mission to Oleshky would involve demining roads leading into the town, delivering food and evacuating civilians. “A sufficient quantity of humanitarian aid will be delivered to meet the needs of everyone who requires it. What’s more, we are working to ensure that this is not just a one-off event, and that it is not limited to Oleshky alone,” he said.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian forces continue to report widespread disruptions to the Starlink satellite network, despite Donald Trump’s claim that Elon Musk had lifted restrictions on the service.

The slowdown, which has affected the communications system used by Ukrainian troops, began last week after Trump and Elon Musk, the founder of Starlink, publicly criticised Zelenskyy over continued strikes on Russian oil refineries.

Trump and Musk have denied ordering the slowdown, though the restrictions have raised questions and confusion about who is responsible. Asked about the Starlink slowdowns on Friday, Trump said he would speak to Musk if the restrictions remained in place.

“I’ve heard it was fixed, but if it’s not, I’ll speak to him,” he told reporters.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, “underlined the importance for Ukraine to have full access” to Starlink in a phone call with Trump on Friday, Downing Street said.

Ukrainian officials said throughout the day on Friday that speeds remained capped at about 100mph, with no indication that the restrictions had been lifted.

“At present, we have not observed any lifting of the restrictions on Starlink,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Zelenskyy.

“There have been isolated cases in which Starlink has operated at speeds slightly above the imposed limits, but this is likely due to SpaceX’s algorithms or specific conditions of use, rather than any lifting of the restrictions,” Beskrestnov added.

The speed restrictions have prevented Ukrainian military equipment, including drones, from maintaining a connection to the satellite network when travelling at high speeds, hampering offensive drone operations and efforts to intercept incoming Russian attacks.

The slowing down of Starlink, coupled with Zelenskyy’s complaints that Washington had temporarily suspended intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, has plunged relations between Ukraine and the US to a new low in recent days.

Tensions first flared after Washington’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel, as Trump sought to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections. Maritime tracking data showed that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel was en route to New York on Thursday, and on Friday the Russian deputy prime minister, Alexander Novak, said three tankers were en route to the US and claimed Russian companies could supply 500,000 metric tonnes in October.

Moscow said a fresh round of US-brokered talks aimed at ending the war could take place next month, even as Russia launched another overnight barrage against Ukraine.

The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said on Friday that trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US were expected to resume in Abu Dhabi in November. Previous rounds of negotiations have failed to produce a breakthrough, with Moscow and Kyiv far apart over the terms of any peace settlement.

Among Russia’s maximalist demands are that Ukraine withdraw its forces from territory it still controls in the east of the country, drastically reduce the size of its military and adopt a neutral status that would rule out Nato membership.

Speaking to a Russian state television reporter late on Thursday, Putin once again questioned Ukraine’s sovereignty, echoing claims he has repeatedly made throughout the war. “The lands lost by Kyiv are not their territory, they are Russia’s historical lands,” Putin said.

The Russian president also cited unspecified genetic research to revive his longstanding claim that Russians and Ukrainians were “one people”, before insisting that Moscow would achieve all the objectives of its full-scale invasion.

/us-news/2026/oct/23/democrat-james-tala.headline: Talarico's small-donor campaign more than triples Paxton's fundraising as poll lead holds
/us-news/2026/oct/23/democrat-james-tala.bodyHtml:
James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for the US Senate in Texas, has challenged Elon Musk's attempt to buy political influence in the race, declaring: “Texas is not for sale.”

Talarico held a campaign rally on Friday at the University of Texas at Austin, packing an auditorium at his alma mater with hundreds of students and other supporters, who cheered, whooped and waved campaign signs.

The Presbyterian seminarian's insurgent run against Texas attorney general Ken Paxton – a staunch ally of Donald Trump – has become one of the most closely watched races in next month's midterm elections to decide control of Congress, as Democrats seek their first statewide win since 1994.

Talarico, 37, struck his usual upbeat message on Friday but also pulled no punches in denouncing Paxton – who was impeached by his own party over corruption accusations and had a very public divorce – as the most corrupt politician in the state's history.

“I have a legislative record; Ken Paxton has a criminal record,” said Talarico, a state representative, wearing a dark blue jacket, white open collar shirt and blue jeans. “This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or who puts money in their own. This election is about whether you want a senator who is for Texas or for himself. This election is about whether you want senator who serves you or serves their billionaire mega donors.”

Paxton, he continued, has the ultimate mega donor. “Elon Musk is trying to buy the Senate seat. We just found out that the richest man in the world is almost single-handedly bankrolling this effort to install Ken Paxton in the US Senate and stop the movement that we are building in our state.

“In all likelihood, if you've seen an attack ad on your screens, that was Elon. If you've gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you received a text message saying scary things about me with scary black and white photos, that was Elon too.”

Speaking against the backdrop of a giant Texan state flag and 40 young supporters holding “Talarico” signs, the Democrat said that, where his movement is funded by 1.3 million individuals, Paxton is funded by “one dude”.

In a state where data centres have become an incendiary issue, Talarico said: “Elon Musk wants our land. He wants our water. He wants our tax dollars. He wants his very own personal United States senator. He is trying to buy Texas. But on November 3rd, we are going to deliver a crystal clear message to the world's first trillionaire: Texas is not for sale.”

Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund, which in turn transferred the same amount to Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC supporting Paxton, according to federal filings.

Talarico has offset that outside-spending gap with grassroots fundraising: his campaign says it raised $64m from July through September, more than triple Paxton's total, with 97% of donations under $100 each.

Talarico told the crowd that super PACs and “billionaire mega-donors” are spending $200m in the most expensive Senate race in US history to defeat his grassroots campaign. “Big money is powerful, but it is nothing compared to people power,” he insisted, invoking biblical imagery comparing his supporters to “the slingshot” that David used to defeat Goliath.

Talarico returned to the trail after a turbulent month in what has emerged as America's biggest battleground state, having fallen ill with the flu at the end of September and not been seen in public for nine days.

Donald Trump, who nicknames the Democrat “Tala-freako”, claimed without evidence at a rally in San Antonio that Talarico is vegan and had fallen ill because he tried eating meat for political purposes. That baseless claim quickly metastasised into an online rumour that Talarico had checked into a mental health facility in Ohio. It was comprehensively debunked.

Meanwhile the Wall Street Journal published a video showing Paxton celebrating New Year's Eve in Dubai with two US fugitives, Anosh Ahmed and Sameer Suhail, who were indicted in Illinois on healthcare-fraud charges. Ahmed donated $190,000 to Paxton, including $25,000 after his indictment.

Back on the campaign trail, Talarico set out on a “Clear Eyes, Full Hearts” tour of the state, holding a CNN town hall with sceptical Republicans and independent voters.

Paxton, meanwhile, launched an 18-day bus tour of Texas aimed at conservative voters, with the slogan “Come and Take It”, an attack on what he called the far left. Republicans sought to tie Talarico to positions on transgender issues that have proved potent in conservative campaigning.

The campaign enters its final stretch with the Democrat holding a narrow polling advantage: the RealClearPolitics average for polls conducted from 6 to 19 October put Talarico ahead by 1.8 percentage points, and an Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media survey released on Thursday found that 48% of voters support Talarico while 46% favour Paxton.

Early voting began on 19 October, giving both campaigns an immediate test of their ability to mobilise supporters. Talarico voted earlier on Friday.

Supporters at Friday's rally expressed optimism that Talarico's message could signal a new political era for the Lone Star State, along with growing frustration with incumbent Republican officials such as Paxton.

Alina Anil, a 19-year-old student at the University of Texas, who had already cast her ballot, said she attended the event to see Talarico in person and demonstrate her support.

“We've been red for a long time and nothing has really come out of it,” Anil said. “As a student, I don't think there's been a lot of changes in Texas. We need some change and James Talarico seems promising. He was a teacher before, so I have faith in that and I have faith in him.”

Dakota Walker, 31, a pediatric physical therapist, arrived wearing a custom T-shirt reading “Talafrico: Talarico refreshing for Texas”, in the style of the Topo-Chico brand of sparkling mineral water.

“What's not to like about him, what's not to love about him, honestly?” Walker said. “He has morals, he has values, he's an overall good human being and I think we need a drastic change.

“I have to spend so much of my time fighting for my kids, making sure that they get what they need when a family with a child with a disability or different abilities shouldn't have to do that. I know we need healthcare reform and he is very big on that.”

Texas Democrats have come close before without winning: former congressman Beto O'Rourke lost a race to Republican Sen. Ted Cruz in 2018 by less than 3 percentage points.

Asked what a Democratic statewide victory would mean, Walker replied: “Oh man, I'll probably cry, honestly. We need a lot of change and I feel like it's time for a new era.”

Patrick Pearson, 46, an assistive technology professional, said he wanted to back Talarico because of his commitment to policy change. “From everything I've read about him and heard, I think he sounds really awesome,” Pearson said. “He's actually trying to make a change and has a very positive message.”

/world/2026/oct/24/north-korea-new-yalu-.headline: North Korea deepens trade links with China and Russia via two new bridges
/world/2026/oct/24/north-korea-new-yalu-.bodyHtml:
For more than a decade, local Chinese residents pilloried it as nothing more than an empty bridge that led to a North Korean vegetable patch on the other side.

Dozens of trucks are now traversing the bridge linking China to North Korea, boosting trade for the reclusive regime – though the crossing has also triggered concern that it could intensify a struggle for influence over the North between Beijing and the region's other major power, Russia.

The New Yalu River Bridge, which connects the north-eastern Chinese city of Dandong with Sinuiju in North Korea, has four lanes and stretches 3km (1.9 miles) across the Yalu river, and is expected to ease congestion on the ageing Friendship Bridge nearby.

The crossing opened on 15 October, about a month after North Korea and Russia opened another major crossing: the first road bridge across their short shared border, the Yakov Novichenko Bridge – a development reportedly made Chinese officials uneasy, coming on top of signs from the North Korean leader Kim Jong-un that he is prioritising ties with Moscow.

“China's interest in buttressing its influence in North Korea is certainly reinforced by the diversifying North Korea-Russia relationship — ties that China tolerates but watches closely as they add complexity to its relationship with its provocative neighbour,” says Carla Freeman, director of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies' Foreign Policy Institute.

Since late 2024, the North Korean leader has sent ammunition and as many as 16,000 troops to support Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine, and has held two summits with the Russian president in the past three years; in 2024 the two leaders signed a mutual defence pact requiring each country to come to the other's aid if attacked.

In return for arms and combat soldiers, Pyongyang is getting hard currency, real-time battlefield experience for its troops, weapons technology and the chance to extend political and economic cooperation beyond its traditional ally, China.

North Korea stands to benefit from the increased trade, though for China the bridge may carry more geopolitical than economic value, given how little trade it does with its neighbour compared with its other partners.

The insular regime in Pyongyang is nonetheless thought to be wary of deepening its economic dependence on China, by far its biggest trading partner and aid donor, and may still resent Beijing's past support for UN sanctions targeting the North's nuclear weapons programme.

In the past two years, however, Russian and Chinese enforcement of UN sanctions has collapsed, giving North Korea more room to trade. “The main restriction on trade with North Korea is not the infrastructure but international sanctions,” says Justin Hastings, a professor of international relations and comparative politics at Sydney University. “However, because China's enforcement of UN sanctions has become desultory and Russia has actively repudiated their enforcement, North Korea is in a position to benefit from increased trade and weapons help (at least from Russia).”

The North's open border with China contrasts with the one it shares with South Korea: in 2024 the North said it would sever all rail and road links with its neighbour, months after Kim said he would abandon the goal of peaceful reunification and declared South Korea his country's “principal enemy”.

Fyodor Tertitskiy, a North Korea expert at Korea University in Seoul, believes neither China nor Russia can influence North Korea in any meaningful way, pointing to Kim's refusal to surrender his nuclear weapons or moderate his iron grip on power – two changes that would be welcomed in both Moscow and Beijing.

“Both countries understand that Kim Jong-un would rather accept a complete breakdown in relationships than submit,” he says. “So I doubt we are seeing a straightforward struggle for influence. Kim is trying to play the two against each other, but China and Russia are not rivals like the Soviet Union and China were in the 1970s.”

Kim is more likely to turn to China to improve his country's struggling economy, while Beijing is eager to revive its role as the North's biggest influence, according to Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul.

“After expanding military cooperation with Russia … Kim Jong-un is leveraging his windfall from Moscow for additional gains from Beijing. China may seek to recover lost influence by increasing trade and people-to-people exchanges, but the Kim regime prizes autonomy and wants to limit foreign ideological and cultural influences.”

The South Korean government said last year that at least 17 active road and rail links already connect North Korea and China along their 1,400 km-long border.

Tertitskiy is “not particularly optimistic” that the increased contact the bridges bring will improve the lives of ordinary North Koreans or lead to a more western-style economy. “I think it will make reform even less likely. Why pursue reforms and take risks when you can just get what you need from abroad?”

Analysts say the expected rise in trade across the Yalu bridge is likely to be modest at first, but it could become a bellwether for the state of Sino-North Korean ties, says Easley.

“China remains economically indispensable to North Korea in ways that Russia cannot replace,” he says, adding, “In that sense, the bridge may offer an inadvertent window into bilateral relations if flows are visibly interrupted in the future.”

/media/2026/oct/24/blue-planet-iii-cloud.headline: Blue Planet III deliberately keeps its footage looking real, not AI
/media/2026/oct/24/blue-planet-iii-cloud.bodyHtml:
The David Attenborough-narrated series Blue Planet III is deliberately leaving in cloudier, less polished footage to counter AI fakery and assure viewers it is “authentic”, its producers have said.

Nearly a decade after Blue Planet II shone a light on plastic pollution, and 25 years since the first Blue Planet aired, the hit BBC series returns with more animal behaviour and cutting-edge technology, including the world's first underwater CCTV camera – dubbed the “stonefish” cam.

Producers have chosen to include more “organic” footage and less polished shots to show that the animals are not AI-generated, after concluding that the rise of AI and the extraordinary, almost fantastical creatures captured by BBC Studios' natural history unit for this series made greater authenticity necessary – even as TVs and cameras have evolved since the first Blue Planet to give viewers sharper, higher-definition pictures.

The executive producer, Elizabeth White, said AI “makes us want to be even more authentic”, adding that the creatures filmed in the deep ocean “are probably more remarkable than AI could imagine and it's completely real”.

She said that in the past “the amount of plankton and things that are in the water in the sequences” would usually mean they might be excluded, and previously, “we might have framed out a boat or a buoy or gone: ‘Oh, actually … the water conditions are not really good enough for this.’”

Now, such things are being left in, as “we're really leaning into that authenticity … As AI booms we will probably lean more into the more organic”, murkier and less polished footage.

For the first time, the BBC's specialist factual commissioning head, Jack Bootle, assured journalists at a press screening: “No gen AI was used in this series. Not a single frame. It's all real photography.”

Bootle added that we live in a “golden age of natural history-making … sometimes people feel like they've seen it all before [so] this series is bursting with novel behaviour”.

Among the never-before-seen footage is action of dolphins using sea sponges to block holes in coral to trap fish, captured using underwater CCTV developed by the programme's producer and director, Yoland Bosiger.

Over four years of filming across five oceans, BBC Studios “continually innovated”, said the series producer, Lara Bickerton: creating a “mini-dome” camera to follow an octopus, a “deep-sea selfie stick”, leg-mounted scooters for camera operators to capture immersive TikTok-style diving footage, and lasers to film deep-sea creatures.

Other remarkable animal behaviour captured in the programme includes grouper communicating with another species of fish; 200,000 crabs lining up in formation to feed; sea urchins using shells as sun hats; and penguin footage that echoes the Planet Earth II, ‘iguana v snakes’ sequence.

The series also addresses threats to the ocean alongside its resilience: episodes show how the climate crisis is killing off the sea where anemone clown fish live and what they do to try to fix their homes, while the plastics story raised in Blue Planet II continues with one about pollutants [and] forever chemicals, said White.

Bosiger said Attenborough, who is 100 years old, was “very much involved” and made changes to scripts.

White added: “What's wonderful is he hasn't lost his curiosity … he's still that little boy … who gets excited … when you show him a new piece of footage.”

Asked if the BBC's £500m cost-cutting drive would affect BBC Studios' renowned natural history reputation, White pointed out that Blue Planet III made savings by using more local crews on location than in previous series, though she said she could not comment further.

  • Blue Planet III starts Sunday 1 November on BBC1 and iPlayer
